sentences.text: Dracovenator was a medium-sized, ground-dwelling, bipedal carnivore estimated to reach 5.5 to 6.5 meters in length and 250 kilograms in mass.
This animal possessed a distinct kink in its upper jaws located between the maxilla and the premaxilla.
The raised shape of its premaxilla makes Dracovenator unique within its family.
The posterior end of its lower jaw features a variety of masses or protuberances.
Some estimates suggest Dracovenator was the largest member of the family Dilophosauridae, reaching 7 meters in length.
Adam M. Yates described and named the genus Dracovenator in 2005, with the type species Dracovenator regenti formally described in 2006.
The genus name Dracovenator is a contraction of the Latin words for dragon and hunter, meaning dragon hunter or dragon catcher.
The species name D. regenti honors the late Regent Lucas Huma, who was a field assistant to Professor Kitching.
James Kitching and Regent Lucas Huma discovered the holotype at the Granja Drumbo Superior locality in the Elliot Formation.
The type material was discovered at the Upper Drumbo Farm locality in the upper Elliot Formation in the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa.
The paratype specimen was discovered by Munyikwa and Raath in 1999, while another paratype was found in 1981.
Researchers believe Dracovenator fed on prosauropods in its paleoenvironment.
Yates assigned Dracovenator to the clade Neotheropoda and classified it within the family Dilophosauridae.
Cladistic analysis indicates that Dracovenator forms a clade with the basal theropods Dilophosaurus and Zupaysaurus.
Dracovenator lived from the Hettangian to the Sinemurian, between 201.4 and 192.9 million years ago.
Fossils of Dracovenator are housed at the Bernard Price Institute for Palaeontological Research in Johannesburg, South Africa.
